title: Chapter 6 | The Two AI Winters
text: CHAPTER 6 The Two AI Winters For most of the twentieth century, the dream of artificial intelligence sparkled with promise—and regularly collapsed under its own weight. The First AI Winter In the early days, researchers believed that to build an intelligent machine, all one had to do was program in the facts. If you could load a database with enough data about the world, surely intelligence would emerge. It didn’t. The first major efforts at AI were logic-based, rule-bound systems. These “expert systems” worked in narrow domains, such as diagnosing car trouble or medical conditions—so long as all the relevant information was hand-coded into the system. But the real world is messy. It’s full of nuance, contradiction, and edge cases. The failure of these early models became apparent, and expectations plummeted. This disappointment marked the first AI winter in the 1970s—a deep freeze in funding, credibility, and academic interest. The Second AI Winter But hope is persistent. Artificial intelligence in the 1970s and early 1980s was dominated by symbolic approaches—systems that relied on logic, search trees, and hand-coded rules to simulate intelligence. These systems achieved early success in constrained domains such as game playing and expert systems, but they struggled with ambiguity, perception, and the messy, continuous nature of real-world data. As these limitations became clearer, frustration grew. Yet an older idea quietly resurfaced. Decades earlier, in the 1950s and 1960s, pioneers such as Frank Rosenblatt had introduced the perceptron—a simplified model of a neuron that could learn to recognize patterns. But the limitations of early neural networks were sharply criticized in a 1969 book by Marvin L. Minsky and Seymour Papert, which pointed out that single-layer networks couldn’t solve even basic logical functions. 32 Then, in the mid-1980s, that story changed. A small group of researchers—including Geoffrey Hinton (we spoke about him earlier), David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams—revived the field with a powerful updated insight: If you stacked multiple layers of simple neuron-like units and trained them using a technique called backpropagation, a training method that computes how wrong the network’s outputs are and then adjusts each layer’s connections to reduce that error, these neural networks could, in principle, learn rich internal representations of complex data. It was a breakthrough—not in biology but in computation. And it reflected how our biological intelligence works. It is not surprising that Hinton would lead this journey in the breakout of AI. He earned his bachelor of arts in experimental psychology from the University of Cambridge in 1970. And then he received his PhD in artificial intelligence from the University of Edinburgh in 1978. His doctoral research was focused on how the human brain might represent knowledge and perform learning—topics deeply rooted in cognitive science and early computational neuroscience. These new artificial neural networks were still primitive by today’s standards—slow to train, limited in scale, and dependent on modest datasets. But they captured a radical possibility: that learning didn’t require encoding knowledge by hand. It might instead emerge from exposure, feedback, and the adjustment of connections over time. Much in the same way that we learned that our DNA does not pass on knowledge specifics so much as a learning infrastructure. For a moment, optimism surged. But the technology was ahead of its time. Computing power was limited, and the available data was insufficient to demonstrate the neural networks’ full potential. Once again, progress stalled. Public interest waned, funding dried up, and by the early 1990s, artificial intelligence entered its second major winter. But behind the scenes, something quiet was happening: Computing power was accelerating, data access was multiplying because of the internet, and researchers—many working in the margins—continued to refine the architectures and ideas that would eventually lead to a profound resurgence. The seeds of deep learning had been planted. They just needed time to grow. But as computing power exploded, things began to change. OceanofPDF.com
